newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ economy "not falling into deep, dark hole" -ANZ.
newsitem.headline: NZ economy "not falling into deep, dark hole" -ANZ.

text.p: The risks of a sharper than expected economic slowdown in New Zealand are real but should not be overstated, ANZ Banking Group economists said in a quarterly report published on Thursday.
Chief economist in New Zealand, Paul Stewart, said conditions would remain subdued, profits would be under pressure, unemployment would rise and confidence fall.
"However, this does not mean the economy is falling into a deep, dark hole," he said.
The economy would remain soft for the next 3-6 months and there could even be a quarter of negative growth.
But the impact of easier monetary conditions, lower interest and exchange rates and stronger world growth with lift growth in 1998.
The bank forecasts 1.7 percent GDP growth in the March 1998 year, down from ANZ's March forecast of 2.1 percent. But growth would pick up to 3.2 percent the following year.
Stewart said New Zealand's economic fundamentals had not changed significantly.
"We see no compelling reason to significantly change our assessment of the economic outlook."
"There are sound reasons to remain optimistic about the medium-term."
These include firmer world growth, a fiscal stimulus and easier monetary conditions.
ANZ said it saw interest rates easing further even after a three percentage point fall from their 1996 peak.
"We expect (the Reserve Bank) to sanction a further, modest, easing in monetary policy (say equivalent to 0.5 percent in interest rates) at the end of June."
ANZ expects short-term rates to edge down in the 6.5-7.0 percent range over the next few months.
